title: Dividend Policy
subtitle: Pay a dividend or retain earnings for reinvestment?
openingQuestion: Why do many high-growth companies not pay dividends?
openingOptions: Because reinvestment opportunities earn a higher return - keeping the cash grows the business better than returning it
explanation: Dividend policy answers the question of whether the remaining profit should be kept or returned to shareholders, and the answer depends on a single comparison: does the business still have reinvestment opportunities earning more than the cost of capital? If so, retaining it creates more value; if not, retaining it only dilutes efficiency. One important practical point: the market reads a dividend as a promise, so cutting it is a very strong negative signal.

diagram.label: Is there still reinvestment with ROIC above the cost of capital?
Yes: retain it, growth creates more value
No: return it to shareholders via dividends or buybacks

realWorldExample.description: Amazon paid no dividend for over 20 years - all its FCF was reinvested into AWS, Marketplace, Prime. As the cloud segment matures, shareholder pressure for dividends and buybacks has increased.

quiz.question: What does a dividend yield of 3% mean?
options: The share price rises 3% each year thanks to the dividend policy
Dividends account for 3% of after-tax profit
Buy 100 units of stock and receive 3 units of dividend each year
The company distributes 3% of outstanding shares as a dividend
quiz.explanation: Dividend yield = DPS / Price = 3% → buy 100 units of stock, receive 3 units of dividend/year. Utilities and REITs usually have a high yield (4-6%). Tech usually 0-1%.

quiz.question: Why is a company's dividend policy usually far 'stickier' (changing less) than its actual profit, which can swing wildly quarter to quarter?
options: Because accounting profit fluctuates but cash flow doesn't change
Because regulations require holding dividends flat for three years
Because dividends are calculated on paid-in capital, not on profit
Because the market reads a dividend cut as a bad long-term signal
quiz.explanation: This is 'dividend smoothing' - the phenomenon of companies trying to keep dividends stable or steadily increasing, avoiding cuts unless truly forced to, because the market views a dividend cut as a very negative signal about long-term financial health.

quiz.question: When should a business retain earnings instead of paying dividends?
options: When ROIC is still higher than the business's cost of capital
When the share price is falling and cash is needed to support it
When the business wants to reduce its debt-to-equity ratio
When major shareholders have no need for cash this year
quiz.explanation: Retaining a unit of profit is only worthwhile if the business turns it into more than a unit of value. If ROIC is below the cost of capital, that unit should go to shareholders so they can invest it elsewhere.

quiz.question: Dividend of 2,000 VND/share, price 50,000 VND. What is the dividend yield?
options: 25x (= 50,000 ÷ 2,000, inverting numerator and denominator)
4% (= 2,000 ÷ 50,000, dividend divided by price)
2% (= 2,000 ÷ 100,000, wrong share price)
40% (= 2,000 ÷ 5,000, off by a decimal place)
quiz.explanation: Yield = 2,000/50,000 = 4%. This is on the high side, typical for utilities or property-for-rent - but a high yield can also come from a recently fallen share price, not a recently increased dividend.

quiz.question: A fast-growing tech company usually has a dividend yield near zero. Why?
options: Because its profit is mostly paper profit
Because regulations don't allow tech companies to pay dividends
Because it still has many reinvestment opportunities earning a high return
Because its shareholders face a higher dividend tax rate than other sectors
quiz.explanation: Every unit retained is creating more than one unit of value, so returning it to shareholders is wasteful. Once those opportunities run out, those same companies start paying dividends - a signal about the stage of maturity.

keyTakeaways: Retain earnings if ROIC > cost of capital
Pay dividends when investment opportunities have dried up

practicePrompt.question: A company has ROIC (return on invested capital) = 18%, while its Cost of Capital (WACC) is only 10%. Management is weighing: should it pay out all profit as dividends, or retain it for reinvestment? Which decision creates more value?
options: The company should retain the profit and reinvest it, because ROIC of 18% exceeds the 10% cost of capital
Should pay out all profit as a dividend immediately because shareholders always prefer cash over letting the company reinvest
ROIC and Cost of Capital have nothing to do with the decision to pay a dividend or retain earnings
This decision should be based purely on management's preference, without comparing ROIC to Cost of Capital
practicePrompt.explanation: Retain earnings if ROIC > cost of capital: when a company can reinvest and generate a return (18%) higher than its cost of capital (10%), retaining profit for reinvestment creates more value for shareholders than paying a dividend - this is the logic behind the dividend policy of high-growth companies.

summary.keyIdea: Retain earnings if ROIC > cost of capital
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: Pay dividends when investment opportunities have dried up

application.title: Apply it now
application.message: If you have idle cash, ask yourself: what would create more value than 'just holding the cash' - learning a skill, investing, paying off high-interest debt? That's the ROIC vs. cost of capital question at a personal scale.
application.secondary: Amazon skipped dividends for a decade to reinvest - you can apply the same logic to your own wallet.

sections.text: When a business has profit, the next question is: return it to shareholders immediately as a dividend, or retain it for reinvestment to create more value in the future? The answer depends on a simple but decisive comparison: ROIC versus the cost of capital.
The core principle: ROIC versus the cost of capital

If a business's ROIC (return on invested capital) is higher than its cost of capital, retaining money for reinvestment creates more value than paying it out as dividends and letting shareholders find their own investments. This is exactly why Amazon didn't pay dividends for over 20 years - all its free cash flow was reinvested into AWS, its logistics network, and Prime, segments with an outstanding ROIC. Conversely, once growth slows and high-return investment opportunities dry up, a business starts paying dividends - as Microsoft did starting in 2003 when its revenue growth flattened.
Why dividends are usually 'stickier' than actual profit

A company's profit can swing sharply every quarter, but dividend policy is usually stable or steadily increasing - a phenomenon called 'dividend smoothing'. The reason: the market reacts very negatively to a dividend cut, seeing it as a bad signal about the company's long-term outlook. So management usually only raises the dividend when confident it can be sustained long-term, and tries to avoid cutting it at almost any cost, even if profit temporarily declines.

items: Dividend yield = Dividend per share (DPS) / Share price - measures the cash return relative to the value invested
Utilities and REITs usually have a high dividend yield (4-6%) because they have fewer high-growth reinvestment opportunities
Growth tech companies usually have a low dividend yield (0-1%) because they prioritize reinvestment
Cutting a dividend usually causes a share price decline larger than the corresponding profit decline

lines: Paying a dividend isn't a sign a company is 'better' - it's just a sign the company has run out of high-return reinvestment opportunities.
